original_question: Can mitochondrial diseases be caused by mutations that interfere with the creation of proton gradients across the mitochondrial membrane?

final_qi.question: Can mitochondrial diseases be caused by mutations that interfere with the creation of proton gradients across the mitochondrial membrane?
final_qi.long_answer: A core function of the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Complexes I, III and IV) is to pump protons from the matrix to the inter-membrane space, establishing an electrochemical proton gradient that is then used by ATP synthase (Complex V) to make ATP. Mutations in mitochondrial DNA or in nuclear genes that encode subunits or assembly/co-factor proteins for these complexes can impair proton pumping or proton motive force formation. When the gradient is insufficient, oxidative phosphorylation fails, ATP production drops, and cells—especially those with high energy demand—dysfunction, producing the clinical phenotypes grouped as mitochondrial diseases. Well-documented examples include:  • mtDNA point mutations in the ND genes of Complex I causing Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) and Leigh syndrome; these mutations reduce proton translocation efficiency. • Nuclear-encoded SURF1 mutations that impair Complex IV assembly, collapsing the proton gradient and leading to Leigh syndrome. • m.8993T>G/C mutations in ATP6 (part of Complex V proton channel) that uncouple proton flow from ATP synthesis, producing Neuropathy-Ataxia-Retinitis Pigmentosa (NARP) and maternally inherited Leigh syndrome (MILS). These and many other documented pathogenic variants demonstrate that interference with proton-gradient creation is a well-established mechanism underlying mitochondrial disease. Hence, mutations that disturb formation of the mitochondrial proton gradient can and do cause mitochondrial disorders.

0.question: What are mitochondrial diseases and what causes them?

final_answer.long_answer: Several inherited mitochondrial disorders arise from mutations in genes encoding respiratory-chain complexes (I, III, IV, V) or their assembly factors. These mutations impair electron transport–driven proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane, collapse the proton-motive force, and thereby limit ATP synthesis. Examples include complex I deficiencies (e.g., NDUFS2 mutations), complex III deficiency (e.g., BCS1L mutations), and ATP synthase (complex V) disorders such as MT-ATP6 mutations that cause Leigh syndrome. Thus, disruption of proton-gradient formation is a well-established pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial disease.
